title: Contra Arianos Dialogus Probo Judice Interlocutoribus
author: Vigilius of Thapsus

passages.original: 118 Cum in manus strenui lectoris, beatissime papa Materne, liber iste a catholico sacerdote et probatissimae vitae beato Athanasio, contra hæreticos Sabellium, Pbotinum et Arium, disputatus pervenerit, illico respondebit : Et quomodo fieri potest ut cum sanclo Athanasio successore beati Alexandri episcopi habuerit Arius conflictum , cum constet eum, sicut in ecclesiastica Historia legitur, turpissima morte, id est, exemplo Judæ traditoris Domnini nostri Jesu Cbristi, fuisse fusum : ut quod fetida mente conceperat ,fetido terminaret fine. Sed si illud recolat, quod in Chronicis suIs beatne memoriae Sulpicius Severus posuit dicens: Duo Arii , tanquam duo urpentes, ex uno ore sibilabant : duos Arios fuisse evidenter reperiet. Unde intelligitur, aut cum Ario superstite, non cum illo qui fusus est, aut cum aliquo Ariomanita sanctum Alhanasium habuisse conflictum.
passages.english: When this book, the disputation held by the blessed Athanasius, a catholic bishop of most approved life, against the heretics Sabellius, Photinus and Arius, comes into the hands of an energetic reader, most blessed Pope Maternus, he will immediately reply: "And how can it be that Arius had a contest with Saint Athanasius, successor of the blessed bishop Alexander, when it is agreed that, as is read in the Ecclesiastical History, he died a most shameful death, that is, poured out after the example of Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that what he had conceived with a foul mind he ended with a foul end?" But if he recalls what Sulpicius Severus of blessed memory set down in his Chronicles, saying, "Two Ariuses, like two serpents, hissed from one mouth," he will clearly find that there were two Ariuses. From this it is understood that Saint Athanasius had his contest either with the surviving Arius, not with the one who was poured out, or with some Ariomaniac.
passages.notes: "Fusum" (poured out) refers to Arius' death by his bowels bursting. "Urpentes" read as "serpentes"; "Pbotinum" as "Photinum". The number 118 is a page/column mark from the edition.

passages.original: Et quanquam de hoc superiore prosecutionebreviter pauca perstrinxeris, lata tamen et propria quaestionis hujuscemodi debet esse probatio. Quam tunc copiosius expedire debebis, dum in ter te atque Athanasium disputat onis examen cœperit agitari. Et quoniam nunc (ut dixi) assertione vendica Sabellii est perfidia refulata, fidei sux , Photinus certis, si valet, testimoniis adsit.
passages.english: And although in your preceding argument you have touched briefly on a few points about this, the proof of a question of this kind ought nevertheless to be full and proper. You will have to set it out more amply at the time when the examination of the disputation between you and Athanasius begins to be conducted. And since now (as I said) the perfidy of Sabellius has been refuted by the assertion of the claimant, let Photinus come forward in support of his faith with sure testimonies, if he can.
passages.notes: Several scanning errors corrected: 'prosecutionebreviter' as 'prosecutione breviter', 'in ter' as 'inter', 'disputat onis' as 'disputationis', 'refulata' as 'refutata', 'sux' as 'suae'. 'assertione vendica' is unclear, possibly for 'assertione vindicis' or 'vindicata'; it is rendered tentatively as 'by the assertion of the claimant'.

passages.original: Probus judex dixit : Si ecclesiasticæ consuetudinis mos est ut aliqua verborum vocabula coercendis hæreticorum motibus in fidei auctoritate nuda ponantur, quæ tamen ratione ex consequentia rerum existentium vestiantur; dum eorum veritas ex qua originem sumunt, divinis contineri litteris invenitur, quid dicis, Ari? Concedis homousion (sicut Athanasius dicit) de divinis Scripturis per convenientes professionis qualitates probari, an non?
passages.english: Probus the judge said: If it is the custom of ecclesiastical usage that certain terms are set down bare in the authority of the faith to restrain the movements of heretics, terms which are nevertheless clothed by reason from the consequence of existing things, provided that their truth, from which they take their origin, is found to be contained in the divine writings, what do you say, Arius? Do you grant that the homoousion (as Athanasius says) is proved from the divine Scriptures through fitting qualities of profession, or not?
passages.notes: Homousion: the Nicene term 'of one substance'.

passages.original: Age nunc, jain si videtur, a terrenis ac visibilibus in superiora mentis oculum erigamus, et ex his quae facta sunt, infectae virtutis substantiam cognoscamus, apostolicæ auctoritatis edocli magisterio, quo dicit invisibilem 148 Divinitatis virtutem ex his quæ facta sunt debere intelligi (Rom. I, 20). Dicit ergo Arius, Filium ex Paire natum esse , et neunt Deum genuisse, lucem lucem. In qua professione unum erit e duobus proculdubio retinendum. Aut enim ex seipso generans id quod ipse est genuit, et ob hoc Filius cum Patre unius substantiæ erit.
passages.english: Come now, if it seems good, let us raise the eye of the mind from earthly and visible things to higher ones, and from the things that have been made let us come to know the substance of the unmade power, taught by the instruction of apostolic authority, by which [the Apostle] says that the invisible power of the Godhead ought to be understood from the things that have been made (Rom. 1:20). Arius, then, says that the Son was born from the Father, and that God begot God, light [begot] light. In this profession one of two things must without doubt be held. For either, generating from himself, he begot that which he himself is, and for this reason the Son will be of one substance with the Father.
passages.notes: "neunt" read as "Deum". The number 148 is an edition page mark, omitted.

passages.original: Volente igitur Deo, corruptibilisnaturæ Virgo sine ullo corruptionis vitio generavit: et ipse qui incorruptibilior cunctis naturis incorruptibiliter praestitit generare, hoc sibi praestare non potuit, ut de sua substantia Filium incorruptibiliter generare potuerit? Ergo quia Deum de seipso Filium generasse et divinarum Scripturarum testantur eloquia, et in sua id Arius superiore prosecutione fassus est, judica (virorum optime Probe) quis magis cum divinisconveniat Scripturis, utrumne ego, qui ob hoc unius substantiæ Filium cum Patre esse profiteor,quod videlicet ex ipso, et non aliunde dignoscitur natus: et ob hoc rursum incorruptibiliter genuisse profiteor, quia excellentssima divinæ majestatis substantia per sui ineffabilem152 potentiam corruptioni subjacere non potest.An is e qui in tanto ancipitis intelligentiae discrimine posttus est, ut quo fidei suae pedem ponat nesciat.
passages.english: By God's will, then, a Virgin of corruptible nature gave birth without any flaw of corruption; and could he who granted her to give birth incorruptibly, he who is more incorruptible than all natures, not grant this to himself, that he could beget a Son incorruptibly from his own substance? Therefore, since both the utterances of the divine Scriptures testify that God begot the Son from himself, and Arius admitted this in his earlier argument, judge, Probus, best of men, who agrees more with the divine Scriptures: whether I, who profess that the Son is of one substance with the Father precisely because he is recognised to have been born from him and not from elsewhere, and who again profess that he begot incorruptibly because the most excellent substance of the divine majesty, through its ineffable power, cannot be subject to corruption; or he who is placed in such a crisis of uncertain understanding that he does not know where to set the foot of his faith.
passages.notes: The final sentence is an incomplete comparison in the Latin ("An is..."), continued in the following passage. The number 152 is an edition page mark.

passages.original: Et idcirco unius fatemur esse substantiae, quia non aliunde, non ex nihilo, non ex subjacentibus vel praecedentibus materiarum qualitatibus ; sed proprie Deum de Deo, lumen de lumine, virtutem de virtute, sapientiam de sapientia fideliter exslitisse fatemur. Nam si alterius ac diversæ substantiae (ut Arius arbitratur) Filius esset, non diceret: SiMul habel Pater vitam in semetipso, sic dedit et Filio vitam habere in semetipso (Joan. v, 26); et iterum : Sicut Pater novit me, et ego novi Patrem (Joan.
passages.english: And therefore we confess [him] to be of one substance, because [he is] not from elsewhere, not from nothing, not from underlying or preceding qualities of materials; but we faithfully confess that he came forth properly God from God, light from light, power from power, wisdom from wisdom. For if the Son were of another and different substance (as Arius supposes), he would not say: "As the Father has life in himself, so he has given also to the Son to have life in himself" (John 5:26); and again: "As the Father knows me, and I know the Father" (John
passages.notes: "Simul" is read as "Sicut"; the citation is completed in the following context (10:15).

passages.original: Quod cum ita sit, Aulus jam intentatæ quæstionis relinquitur locus qua quæriiur utrum voluntate Deus Pater, an natura Filium generaverit; cum in Deo (ut perdocuimus) non aliud sit voluntas quam sapientia, nec aliud sapientia quam natura, quae virtus etiam appellatur. Et cum hæc omnia Christus sit, sicut ait Apostolus : Nos autem prædicamus Christum Dei virtutem, et Dei sapientium ( I Cor. 23, 24), apparet cum libera naturalis virtutis omnipotentia ex Patre genitum esse; quoniam natura in Deu, non ut Arius ridicule opinatur, necessitatis conditione putatur (ne et ipse Pater, qui naturaliter subsistit, es necessitate subsistere videatur); sed cst liberæ potestatis, et nullus vincta necessitatibus virtus;
passages.english: Since this is so, no room is now left for the question raised, in which it is asked whether God the Father begot the Son by will or by nature; since in God, as we have fully shown, will is nothing other than wisdom, and wisdom nothing other than nature, which is also called power. And since Christ is all these things, as the Apostle says, "But we preach Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Cor. 1:23–24), it is evident that he was begotten from the Father by the free omnipotence of natural power; since nature in God is not thought of, as Arius absurdly supposes, as a condition of necessity (lest the Father himself too, who subsists by nature, should seem to subsist by necessity); but it is of free power, and a power bound by no necessities;
passages.notes: "Aulus" read as "nullus"; "cum libera" taken as "eum libera". The reference "I Cor. 23, 24" should be 1 Cor. 1:23–24.

passages.original: Arius dixit: Ego Spiritum sanctum non solum Pa- tre et Filio minorem, verum etiam voluntatis eorum ministrum et obecundatorem confiteor, ut pote crea- Iuram creatori reverentissimum famulatus obsequium præbentem. Qui tamen cunctis creaturis et melior, et post Filium primus sit. Nam si aequalis cum Patre, ut Athanasius profitetur, honoris pilvilegio insignitur, non dicerct Filius quia non loquetur a semetipso, sed quæcunque audierit, loquetur. Qui enim nihil ultronea potestatis auctoritate loquitur, jubentis imperio per obsequium ministerii famulatur.
passages.english: Arius said: I confess that the Holy Spirit is not only less than the Father and the Son, but also the minister and complier with their will, inasmuch as he is a creature offering to the Creator the most reverent obedience of service. Yet he is better than all creatures, and first after the Son. For if he were distinguished by the privilege of honour equal with the Father, as Athanasius professes, the Son would not say that 'he will not speak of himself, but whatever he hears, he will speak.' For one who speaks nothing by the free authority of [his own] power serves the command of one who orders, through the obedience of ministry.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected ('obecundatorem' read as 'obsecundatorem', 'pilvilegio' as 'privilegio', 'dicerct' as 'diceret'). The quotation is John 16:13.

passages.original: Athanasius dixit: Reliquarum quæstionum, quibus Arius opinatur posse Filium a Patre ostendi minorem, principale illud est, quod idem Filius ait, Pater major me est; quod jam cognoscitur intentasse, et huic velut capiti cuncta quæstionum inhaerent membra. Nam quod ait, Non veni facere voluntatem meam (Joan.
passages.english: Athanasius said: Of the remaining questions by which Arius supposes the Son can be shown to be less than the Father, the principal one is what the same Son says, "The Father is greater than I"; which he is known already to have raised, and on this, as on a head, all the members of the questions depend. For as to his saying, "I did not come to do my own will" (John
passages.notes: The passage breaks off mid-reference (John 6:38), continued in the next passage.

passages.original: Ostensum namque est multis et copiosis divinarum lectionum probamentis, et Patrem, et Filium, et Spiritum sanctum, suis specialiter et propriis exstare personis : alium esse genitorem, alium genitum, alium geniti atque ingeniti Spiritum sanctum; licet secundum Athanasii probabilem fidci veritatem , aliud esse non possint, cum alius atque alius credi possint, et profecto sint. Quia enimvero extremæ atque profundæ stultitiæ genus est Patrem nominare eum qui non genuit, et Filium credere eum qui genitus non sit;
passages.english: For it has been shown by many and abundant proofs from the divine readings that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit each exist in their own particular and proper persons: that the begetter is one, the begotten another, and the Holy Spirit of the begotten and the unbegotten another. Yet, according to the commendable truth of Athanasius' faith, they cannot be another thing, though they can be believed to be one and another, and indeed are. For truly it is a kind of extreme and profound folly to name as Father one who has not begotten, and to believe as Son one who has not been begotten;
passages.notes: The distinction is between 'alius' (another person) and 'aliud' (another thing or substance).

passages.original: V. Et ut se Athanasius antiquorum auctoritato muniret, talia priscae consuetudinis exempla protnlit ; quæ Arius non solum negare non posset, verum etiam pari cum eo fidei ratione defenderet. Propo- suit igitur ad demonstrandam super nominum novitatibus antiqui moris regulam, quod contra Sabellium, qui Patrem genitum asserebat, ingenitum atque innascibilem debere catholicos proliteri, praeteritorum conciliorum decreto fuisse initum ;
passages.english: V. And so that Athanasius might fortify himself with the authority of the ancients, he brought forward such examples of ancient custom as Arius not only could not deny, but would even defend with him on the same principle of faith. He therefore set forth, to demonstrate the rule of ancient custom regarding novelties of names, that against Sabellius, who asserted that the Father was begotten, it had been established by decree of past councils that Catholics ought to profess [him] unbegotten and incapable of birth;
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected ('auctoritato' as 'auctoritate', 'protnlit' as 'protulit', 'proliteri' as 'profiteri'). 'Initum' is read as 'established'.

passages.original: cum hoc ipsum evidentius positum, Scripturæ divinæ auctoritate ostendi non posset; sed hoc profitendum, et ipsa rei veritas, et necessitas hæreticæ professionis exigeret. Item Deum de Deo, lumen ei lumine, Filium confitendum, episcopos religionis, quam Arius tradidit sectatores, in Syrmicnsi synodo tradidisse ; quod ipsum etiam simpliciter et specialiter in Scripturis divinis positum inveniri non posse : et quam plura his similia protulit documenta, quæ gestorum serie tenentur expressa ;
passages.english: since this very thing, set down more explicitly, could not be shown by the authority of divine Scripture; but both the truth of the matter itself and the necessity of [countering] the heretical profession required that it be professed. Likewise, [he cited the fact] that the bishops who were followers of the religion that Arius handed down had laid down at the synod of Sirmium that the Son must be confessed as God from God, light from light; and that this very thing also cannot be found set down plainly and specifically in the divine Scriptures. And he brought forward very many proofs similar to these, which are kept recorded in the sequence of the proceedings;
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the first clause refers back to the decree that the Father must be professed unbegotten. "Syrmicnsi" read as "Sirmiensi".

passages.original: fierique non posse aliud eum quam id quod ipse est edidisse , cum et divinae generationis veritas pro sui honoris reverentia id esse credendum exigeret, et rerum naturalium consuetudinis auctoritas invitaret, non posse parentes dissimilis naturae filios procreare. Et ideo secundum Arii sententiam, qui alterius substantiæ quam Pater est Filium asserebat, hoc humano sensui intelligendum posse reliquit, ut si vere Filius in diversitate naturae est, non tam genitus quam factus esse videatur : sitque vacua et inanis Filii Patrisque appellatio, dum specie tenus magis quam veraciter, aut ille genuisse, aut hic natus praedicatur.
passages.english: and that it could not be that he brought forth anything other than what he himself is, since both the truth of the divine generation, out of reverence for its honour, required this to be believed, and the authority of the customary course of natural things urged it, that parents cannot procreate children of a dissimilar nature. And therefore, according to the view of Arius, who asserted that the Son was of another substance than the Father, he left this to be understood by human sense: that if the Son is truly in a difference of nature, he would seem not so much begotten as made; and the names Son and Father would be empty and vain, since the one is proclaimed to have begotten, or the other to have been born, in appearance rather than in truth.
passages.notes: Passage begins mid-sentence, continuing Athanasius' argument reported in indirect speech.

passages.original: IX. Difficilem quoque illam et (ut Arius autumibat) insolubilem quæstionem, quod tres unus Ocus dici, et idem tribus distingui non posse personis intentaverat, ita Athanasius divinae Scripturæ auctoritate dissolvit; ut majori sit absolutione veritatis enodata, quam fuerit per sy'log:smos versutiarum plictilcs involuta.
passages.english: IX. That difficult question too, and, as Arius thought, insoluble one, which he had raised, that the three cannot be called one God, and that the same cannot be distinguished into three persons, Athanasius so resolved by the authority of divine Scripture that it was untangled with a greater resolution of the truth than it had been entangled by the twisting syllogisms of sophistries.
passages.notes: "Ocus" read as "Deus"; "sy'log:smos versutiarum plictilcs" read as "syllogismos versutiarum plectiles".

passages.original: Nam usque adeo Pater, et Filius, et Spiritus sanctus, unius sunt potestatis, uniusque naturæ, ut Sabellius tantam vim conspiciens vcritatis, unam et singularem 196 esse personam putaverit. Sed in tantum non est una persona, sed tres distinctae, ut Arius eos inæquales, et natura dicat esse diversos. Ergo inaequalitas Arii distinctionem indicat personarum.Confusio Sabellii naturæ apertius unionem ostendit. Rursus dum Photinus ad confirmationem sententiæne suæ, qua putat Christum purum hominem esse, illa replicat testimonia quæ idem Christus humanæ conscius naturæ aut locutus est, aut pcregit;
passages.english: For the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit are to such an extent of one power and one nature that Sabellius, seeing such great force of the truth, thought there was one single person. But so far are they from being one person, and so much are they three distinct [persons], that Arius says they are unequal and diverse in nature. Therefore the inequality of Arius indicates the distinction of the persons; the confusion of Sabellius shows more plainly the unity of nature. Again, while Photinus, to confirm his view by which he thinks Christ is a mere man, repeats those testimonies which the same Christ, conscious of his human nature, either spoke or performed;
passages.notes: The final sentence is incomplete, continued in the following passage. The number 196 is an edition page mark.
